title: Dyer v. National By-Products, Inc.
summary: Forbearance of an invalid claim may be consideration when the claimant honestly and fairly believes it valid; the remand left that factual inquiry open.
notes:
Court: Supreme Court of Iowa (1986).

The notes compare Fiege v. Boehm’s paternity settlement, good faith, pleading obligations, and other waivers. Treat those comparisons as boundary questions, not a license to assert a claim known to be false.

sections.Parties: Dyer, an employee who lost a foot in an accident, sued National By-Products, his employer.
sections.Material Facts: Dyer alleged that the employer promised lifetime employment in exchange for his forbearance of a personal-injury claim. The employer disputed the alleged agreement. The claim he said he surrendered was legally invalid under the applicable compensation regime. He was later laid off.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court granted summary judgment for the employer on the ground that the invalid claim could not supply consideration. The Supreme Court of Iowa reversed and remanded. It did not establish that the alleged promise, bargain, or good-faith belief had been proved.
sections.Issue: Can forbearance of a claim lacking legal merit support a settlement bargain when the claimant believes the claim is valid?
sections.Holding: An honest, good-faith belief may make forbearance sufficient despite the claim’s legal invalidity. The claimant’s good faith required further consideration rather than categorical rejection solely for lack of a valid underlying claim.
sections.Reasoning: The policy supporting compromise would be undermined if every settlement depended on later proof that the surrendered claim would have won. The opinion uses Restatement § 74’s distinction between a doubtful claim and a claim believed fairly capable of being determined valid. Objective weakness may bear on whether a professed belief is honest. A knowingly baseless or bad-faith nuisance claim is not insulated by merely calling its abandonment consideration.
